For this past week, however, U.S. startups continued to secure sizable rounds, led by brain-computer interface company Science landing a fresh $400 million. Another seven American companies announced venture or growth funding of $100 million or more, and across the Atlantic, UK-based AI biotech startup Isomorphic Labs landed $5 billion, the largest financing of the week. 1. Science , $400M, neurotech : Science, a startup focused on brain-computer interface technology, and neural engineering, secured $400 million in Series D funding. The round brings total funding to date for the Alameda, California-based company to more than $900 million. 2. Model ML , $250M, AI and fintech : Model ML, an AI platform for financial and professional services, closed on $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. General Atlantic and QED Investors led the round for the three-year-old company, which is based in New York and London. 3. Galvanize Therapeutics , $130M, biotech : Redwood City, California-based Galvanize Therapeutics, a developer of pulsed electric field ablation technologies for oncology and chronic disease, picked up $130 million in Series D funding led by HealthQuest Capital . 4. General Flash , $128M, critical metals : General Flash, a developer of a new method to produce critical metals, announced that it has raised $128 million across seed and Series A rounds from a long list of investors. 5. Ramon.Space , $124M, space tech : Denver-based Ramon.Space, a developer of space computing infrastructure, pulled in $124M in Series B funding led by PSG . 6. Marrow Therapeutics , $120M, biotech : Watertown, Massachusetts-based Marrow Therapeutics, a developer of bone marrow-targeted therapies to treat severe blood disorders, announced its launch with a combined $173 million in Series A and B funding. Orbimed led its $120 million Series B round while Scion Life Sciences and venBio led the $53 million Series A. 7. Noeri , $110M, enterprise AI : Noeri, a developer of self-improving AI for enterprises and researchers, launched with $110 million in initial funding. Menlo Ventures led the round for the Palo Alto-based startup, which was founded by Stanford University computer science professors. 8. Seawolf Therapeutics , $100M, biotech : San Diego-based Seawolf Therapeutics, a biotech startup developing a novel DNA delivery platform, emerged from stealth and announced that it has raised $100 million in funding to date, with Versant Ventures , MPM BioImpact and Novartis Venture Fund as lead investors. 9. BrightAI , $97M, physical AI : BrightAI, a startup developing a sensor, drone and robotics-driven platform to bring continuous observability to infrastructure-heavy industries like power, water, and energy, secured $97 million in new funding. Smith Point Capital led the financing for the Silicon Valley-based company. 10. Vincue , $93M, vehicle intelligence platform : Kansas City-based Vincue, developer of a vehicle lifecycle intelligence platform, closed on $93 million in growth capital led by Wavecrest Growth Partners . And overseas: Isomorphic Labs , $5B, AI and biotech : London-based Isomorphic Labs, a startup that applies AI to drug discovery, secured $5 billion in Series C funding. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the financing for the five-year-old company, which also has offices in Massachusetts and Switzerland. Methodology We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Nov. 14-20, 2026. payload.text: This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here . What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car? Those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look. $73.5M to reflect sunlight from space Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down. To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset. The company recently announced $73.5 million in new funding , bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase . Existing investors Sequoia Capital , Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures , Convective Capital , The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1 . Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark. The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships. The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally , per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records. Related Crunchbase queries: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding Global Cleantech Startup Funding In 2026 $62M to make better breathing a bigger business Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade. The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness company recently announced a $62 million investment from Camino Partners , the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky . Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward. The company markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It says it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years. Intake plans to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful. Its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026 , putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows. Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software. Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026 $12M to bring AI to the garbage-hauling business Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated. San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana , with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital , Harlem Capital and CreativeCo . The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets. TrashLab says its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection. The company says hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform. It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot , a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there. Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026 $10M to let engineers program factories in plain English Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time. Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler. The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures , with participation from Y Combinator , Thin Line Capital , Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor . Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language. Its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get new production lines up and running. The startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027. The investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026 , nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data. Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026 €6.9M to make space experiments more affordable Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget. Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros. The Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC , with participation from Vanagon Ventures , Prototype Capital and EWOR , among other investors. The company describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date. Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions. Customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth. Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite launched in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch. Tumbleweed says its new funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028. Tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026 , compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data shows. payload.text: By David Spreng The financing of the AI buildout is shifting from equity to debt, and those who invested through the telecom bubble may recognize what that shift tends to mean. There is an old story in Stephen Hawking ’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle. Asked what the turtle stands on, she replies that it’s “turtles all the way down.” Her response is what philosophers call infinite regress — a chain of claims in which each one rests on another of the same kind and solid ground never arrives. David Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital. I think of it when I look at the AI buildout because its logic has taken the same shape. Valuations support borrowing, and borrowing builds capacity. The capacity then becomes proof that the valuations were right, so each claim stands on the one beneath it. Over the past year, more of the stack has started running on debt rather than equity, and in my experience, that crossing is the moment the telecom bubble becomes the relevant history given that debt may change how these stories end. Until recently, the AI buildout was largely an equity-financed story, with venture investment reaching record levels. Crunchbase data shows global venture funding totaled $679 billion through the first three quarters of 2026, the highest amount ever recorded for that period. AI companies attracted $102 billion in the third quarter alone, accounting for roughly 64% of global venture funding. A record 27 companies raised rounds of $1 billion or more during the quarter, collectively accounting for about a third of that total. Equity financing carries significant risks, but unlike debt, it generally does not impose fixed repayment obligations. When investments underperform, equity investors typically absorb losses through declining valuations, while companies may retain greater flexibility to pursue their long-term strategies. That debt is now arriving in size. Meta sold $30 billion of bonds last October in one of the largest corporate debt sales on record , then returned for $25 billion more in April , with investors reportedly demanding more compensation the second time. Amazon , Alphabet and Oracle have each borrowed tens of billions of their own , and Meta’s giant Louisiana data-center campus was financed with a record $27 billion bond raised by a joint-venture partner rather than by Meta itself. Morgan Stanley expects the big AI and cloud companies to spend about $3 trillion on infrastructure through 2028, with only about half of it expected to come from their own cash flow. The rest has to come from somewhere, and increasingly I think that somewhere is the bond market and private credit. I watched the earlier version of this from a front-row seat, first as a venture capitalist in the late 1990s and since then as a lender to growth-stage technology companies. Telecom borrowed staggering sums against a demand forecast that was widely repeated and rarely checked, the famous claim that internet traffic was doubling every 100 days . Traffic was actually doubling about once a year, spectacular growth but a fraction of what the borrowing assumed. By 2002 the telecom sector carried roughly $1 trillion in debt , much of which the chairman of the FCC told Congress would never be repaid, and WorldCom had entered what was then the largest bankruptcy in American history . Much of the fiber the industry laid sat dark for years and was finally put to work by buyers who paid pennies on the dollar for it in bankruptcy, through a decade of restructurings and private mergers that rebuilt entire cap tables. Some companies survived that process, and many did not. The demand narrative The echo that concerns me most is the demand narrative. Today’s version holds that data centers are effectively leased before they are built and that the only real mistake is building too little. That may prove correct, but it is repeated with the same uniformity the traffic forecast enjoyed in 1999, and much of it rests on projections supplied by the companies doing the building. What has changed in recent months is that investors have begun demanding an answer. Anthropic is now public, and once companies of that scale report financial results every quarter, investors can check the demand story against audited numbers. Some may argue, reasonably, that my comparison fails and that the companies doing the largest borrowing may be among the most profitable enterprises ever built, with cash flows the telecom carriers never approached. A few AI companies also appear to be reaching revenue scale faster than any businesses before them. And the internet really did change everything, just as the traffic really did arrive. All of that may be true, and none of it answers the question I think a lender has to ask, which is whether the cash arrives on the schedule the debt requires. Equity can generally wait out a wrong timeline in a way debt cannot, and when borrowed money builds capacity faster than revenue arrives to service it, in my opinion, the correction tends to come through restructurings rather than quiet markdowns. Enduring lessons None of this is a prediction that the AI buildout must end the way telecom did. The most durable lesson of the telecom bust, in my view, concerned capital structure, which decided who was still standing when demand finally caught up with capacity, long after the technology itself had been vindicated. I have spent years arguing that growth companies fear debt more than they should , and I still believe it, but the argument has always been conditional. Debt serves borrowers whose obligations are sized to revenue they can see and lenders who underwrite fundamentals instead of narratives, and it treats everyone else harshly. I believe the borrowing stacked beneath the AI boom will be judged by that standard. Every assumption in the stack may well hold, but what I learned the last time is that once investors begin asking what the turtles are standing on, they rarely stop until they reach something solid. David Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital . He has more than 30 years of experience as a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and growth debt lender, has been involved in the formation and development of nearly 50 technology companies, and has appeared four times on the Forbes Midas List of top venture capitalists. He co-founded Decathlon Capital Partners in 2010, served on the board of the National Venture Capital Association and has participated as a panelist at the World Economic Forum in Davos. payload.text: By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge ’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy. And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook. To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation. While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy. The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy. To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units. Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges. Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona , a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge . Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them. Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here . Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria . He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol , among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject. Onetti has a column on Sifted ( Financial Times ) and several other tech blogs.

Top fundraisers Much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers. As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks. By far the largest funding recipient is Mercor , a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation. San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers. The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob , a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce 1 -led financing. Startups focused on jobseekers Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers. In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox , an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation. Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview , a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI , which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding. Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform , announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs. Surprisingly depressing So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers? Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done. Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions. Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation. payload.text: By Richard Anton Panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value. We have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a company that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it. The SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value. This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal. How the markets got it wrong Richard Anton, co-founder and general partner of Oxx. The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked. When OpenAI launched ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025. The market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal. From there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year. As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others. The recovery has been uneven and markets still get it wrong There were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole. That is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April. At my firm, Oxx , we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back. In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike , whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October. The problem with public markets is part of a bigger trend The knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash. It produced the unintended consequence of driving company ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value. The panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private company transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this issue is to recognize there is actually a problem. Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx , a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale. Anthropic priced shares for its upcoming stock market debut at $83 on Wednesday evening, solidly above the expected range of $70 to $78 laid out in its IPO filing. The offering promised to be the public market event of the season, with the Claude creator seeing investor demand for shares well in excess of its capital-raising goals. The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, including 23.6 million from selling shareholders, up from it’s earlier plan to sell just over 800 million shares. At that upgraded size, the offering is bringing in around $80 billion for the company. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, the IPO and private placement total around $106 billion. It’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut. SpaceX , by comparison, raised $86 billion in its June offering. Fast growth but no profits, yet The IPO follows a revenue growth trajectory for the history books. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. Anthropic claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology to date, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. payload.text: Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization ’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services. That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses. Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption. Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company says it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance. As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out. payload.text: By Kenza Zayani In October, reports that OpenAI ‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could. Kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global , based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to company building with founders. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work. Companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology. The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation. The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession. The numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data shows. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025. Notable rounds The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents. The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI , which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management , Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners . San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners , completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital -led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models. Customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV , at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels. Meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners , at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation. Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, New York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing. Beijing-based ModelBest , which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July. Exits Voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne , which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders. In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox , a developer of conversational voice AI technology. The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience , the South Korean company behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21. Looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai , an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram announced plans to acquire Daily , creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework. More recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end. Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme , managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.” After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said. title: unmark
summary: Stop applying to jobs using AI-generated resume

extra.author: grandimam
extra.original_title: Show HN: Stop applying to jobs using AI-generated resume

story_text.value:
When LLMs hands you a resume or pdf it carry markers of how it was made, including the source. You can't see them on the page but applicant tracking systems can read it.

So recruiters are flagging such profiles and rejecting them entirely. I had tested this across 40+ AI models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, etc) to produce a resume and every single file carried a marker.

To solve this problem. I had built a free tool to show what your file says and gives you a cleaned version:

- Drop your resume and get a cleaned copy - Free, no account.

What it doesn't do: it won't rewrite your resume or make AI-sounding wording more human. It only deals with what's hidden in the file.

It's a simple tool, but it feels absolutely necessary now as more people are using AI for generating their entire resume or even editing them. I am the developer, happy to answer any questions.

title: Musset
summary: open-source Scrivener alternative with an AI that never writes

extra.author: julienmarie
extra.original_title: Show HN: Musset, open-source Scrivener alternative with an AI that never writes

story_text.value:
I’m writing my first novel and could not find an app that fit my workflow: quiet like iA Writer, organized like Scrivener, and with AI so I can discuss my book while I write it. It allows me to feel less “alone” and have a sounding board while I write.

- A book is a folder of plain Markdown files. Musset commits to a git repo, tracks versions and drafts without you having to know git.

- Revisions are CriticMarkup inside the text. It manages docx revisions too, so your editor can edit a Word doc and you import their comments.

- PDFs are typeset using Typst, embedded in the app, following each language’s typographic rules.

- Spelling and grammar are checked using LanguageTool, also embedded.

- Mac/Word, WordStar, vi and Emacs keyboard modes.

The AI is optional and uses your Codex or Claude Code CLI. It comments, leaves margin notes, and checks continuity and your chapters against your style rules.

It’s GPL-3.0 and free during the beta. When or if it reaches 1.0, if there is sufficient interest, the idea is to make it a small one-time payment ($9.90). There is a paid sync service (git hosting) that lets you share a book with beta readers and editors.

Download: https://musset.app

I’d love to have some feedback!

title: obfusecate
summary: Lightweight FUSE-based encrypted, compressed filesystem for Linux

extra.author: tgaloppo
extra.original_title: Show HN: Lightweight FUSE-based encrypted, compressed filesystem for Linux

story_text.value:
A personal project for digging deeper into Linux system programming, ObFUSEcate implements a file backed virtual block device that automatically performs compression and encryption as blocks are accessed. This virtual device can be mounted via FUSE (requiring no root privileges) to provide, effectively, a "live" compressed, encrypted archive.

Written in C++, and intended to have minimal dependencies, it has custom 32 bit arithmetic encoding/decoding, ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption, and CRC8 + XOR parity error-correction.

title: Trichroma
summary: a Platformer of Light

extra.author: namirsab
extra.original_title: Show HN: Trichroma, a Platformer of Light

story_text.value:
Hi Hackernews! I just wanted to share a game I've made over a few weeks just as a little side project. Of course it was developed using Agents Engineering. The idea of the game though comes from around 10 years ago, from conversations with my brother: he is an artist and back them he was experimenting with chromatic paintings that looked differently depending on which color of light they were exposed to. A few weeks ago I decided to show my brother what's possible now a days with AI and how we can turn ideas into reality with a fraction of the effort we would have need in the past. The game is a little platformer, meant to be challenging but cute and entertaining, taking inspiration of games like Celeste or Meatboy. Death is part of the game, and light mechanics are introduced over the course of the 63 levels that are available to play.

The development was made fully from my phone with Claude Code, but I invested lots of time on play testing it and I've involved several friends to play it to gather feedback and improve it.

I'd love to hear your feedback and I hope some of you have fun playing it!

title: OpenComputer
summary: an open source alternative to Devin

extra.author: iacguy
extra.original_title: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer.

OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).

We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]).

Two other choices:

- One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient.

Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3].

[1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev

title.value: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin

Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria.

In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.

At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?

If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

title: anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python: v2.12.0
summary:
### Features

* **api:** add the image_dimensions_too_large error code


### Bug Fixes

* **bedrock:** send the user profile ID in the request body

  Amazon Bedrock reads `user_profile_id` from the request body and ignores the `anthropic-user-profile-id` header, so a profile ID given to `AnthropicBedrock` or `AsyncAnthropicBedrock` was not applied. Both clients now move it into the body of Messages requests and no longer send the header. A `user_profile_id` already in the body takes priority over the header.

  Some models on Bedrock do not support user profiles. A request to one of them with a profile ID now fails with a 400 error; before, the ID was ignored. Leave the ID off requests to those models.


### Chores

* **docs:** clarify billing_policy in batches and two billing errors

Both clients now move it into the body of Messages requests and no longer send the header. A `user_profile_id` already in the body takes priority over the header.

title: huggingface/transformers: Release v5.24.0
summary: # Release v5.24.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint ([TML-d24-varloop-research](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research)) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2_loop) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) | [HF Blog Post](https://huggingface.co/blog/inkling2mini) * Add Inkling2 Mini (#51050) by @guarin ### Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. It extends the Apertus language model with the EMU3.5 vision tokenizer for images and WavTokenizer for audio. The EMU3.5 tokenizer is an image-only VQGAN with the same encoder as Chameleon's, and it assigns codes by the largest inner product with the codebook. The media tokenizers turn images and audio into discrete tokens, which the language backbone processes alongside text in a shared input vocabulary. The output vocabulary contains only text tokens, so image and audio generation are not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/apertus1p5) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### WavTokenizer WavTokenizer encodes 24 kHz mono audio into discrete tokens using a single codebook, at 40 or 75 tokens per second depending on the checkpoint, and reconstructs audio from those tokens. `WavTokenizerModel` encodes and decodes, and `WavTokenizerEncoderModel` only encodes. Speech, music/audio and unified checkpoints are available. The 40-token-per-second variant is the audio tokenizer of Apertus 1.5. Training the codec is not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/wavtokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2408.16532) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### Dory Dory is a looped (latent-recurrent) language model from NVIDIA. It uses a normalized-GPT architecture with interleaved sliding-window and full attention layers. A shared block of layers is applied repeatedly, so Dory can spend more compute per token. The loop count can be changed at inference time on the same checkpoint to trade speed against quality. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/dory) | [Paper (nGPT)](https://huggingface.co/papers/2410.01131) * Add Dory model support (#50099) by @shan18 ### HY4-VL HY4-VL (Hunyuan V4 Vision-Language) combines the HYV4 mixture-of-experts text backbone with a vision encoder for image-text and video-text generation. It supports dynamic-resolution visual inputs and uses multimodal rotary position embeddings (mRoPE) to represent temporal and spatial positions. It builds on the Qwen2-VL design and shares its vision patch merger with HunYuan-VL. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/hy_v4_vl) * Add HY4-VL (#50877) by @vasqu ### Omnilingual ASR Omnilingual ASR is a suite of multilingual speech-recognition models from Meta FAIR that covers more than 1,600 languages. Each model pairs a Wav2Vec2-style audio encoder with one of two heads: * **CTC** (`OmniASRForCTC`): a linear projection to the vocabulary, decoded non-autoregressively with greedy CTC. * **Audio language model** (`OmniASRForConditionalGeneration`): audio embeddings are projected into a Llama decoder that generates the transcription. It optionally takes a language code (e.g. `"eng_Latn"`), which generally improves transcription quality. Both variants come in 300M, 1B, 3B and 7B sizes. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/omniasr) | [CTC Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/omniasr_ctc) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2511.09690) * Adding Omnilingual ASR models (#43265) by @ebezzam ### Lara Mini Lara Mini is a multilingual base language model from Translated with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters per token. It is a hybrid of linear-time recurrent layers, sliding-window attention and a few global attention layers, each followed by a fine-grained mixture of experts. The weights are released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license (non-commercial use) in a gated repository. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/lara_mini) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.16956) * Add Lara Mini (#50819) by @ValeGian ### SarvamMLA SarvamMLA is the architecture of Sarvam-105B, a 105B-parameter mixture-of-experts language model from Sarvam AI. It combines Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with sparse MoE routing: 128 routed experts with 8 active per token, plus 1 shared expert. It uses sigmoid routing with group-based top-k selection and YaRN rotary embeddings for contexts up to 131K tokens. The architecture is the same as DeepSeek-V3, with a custom configuration. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/sarvam_mla) * Add SarvamMLA model (sarvamai/sarvam-105b) (#44569) by @aashay-sarvam ### SarvamMoE SarvamMoE is the architecture of Sarvam-30B, Sarvam AI's 30B-parameter mixture-of-experts model. It uses grouped-query attention with QK normalization, and 128 routed experts with 6 active per token, plus 1 shared expert. The architecture is the same as GLM-4-MoE, so the auto classes load it with the GLM-4-MoE implementation and only `SarvamMoEConfig` is specific to SarvamMoE. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/sarvam_moe) * Add SarvamMoE (sarvamai/sarvam-30b) (#51023) by @hmellor ### EXAONE EXAONE covers the EXAONE 3.0, EXAONE 3.5 and EXAONE Deep language models from LG AI Research. Their architecture is the same as Llama, so the auto classes load them with `LlamaModel` and `LlamaForCausalLM`, and only `ExaoneConfig` is specific to EXAONE. The released checkpoints are renamed to the Llama names when loading and back when saving, so they no longer need `trust_remote_code=True`. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/exaone) * Add EXAONE (#50966) by @hmellor ### Model updates * **Ling 3.1 Flash** now loads natively through `BailingHybrid`, like Ling 3.0 in v5.20.0 (#49737) by @icavan * **Beam** gains a `BeamForTokenClassification` head (#50634) by @AymenKallala ## Breaking changes ### Cache renaming: `past_key_values` / `cache_params` → `cache` (#50585, #50730) `past_key_values` and `cache_params` are renamed to `cache` across the library. The old names still work with a deprecation warning; see the dedicated section below. * 🚨🚨 Rename `past_key_values`/`cache_params` to `cache` (#50585) by @Cyrilvallez * Bump minimal peft version for cache name compatibility (#50730) by @Cyrilvallez Attention models used to call their cache `past_key_values`, while Mamba-style and linear-attention models called it `cache_params`. Hybrid models therefore had to juggle two names for the same object. There is now a single name, `cache`, everywhere: model `forward` signatures, `generate`, `prepare_inputs_for_generation`, the masking utilities, and every `ModelOutput`. ```python # Before outputs = model(input_ids, past_key_values=past_key_values, use_cache=True) next_cache = outputs.past_key_values # Now outputs = model(input_ids, cache=cache, use_cache=True) next_cache = outputs.cache ``` * **Fully backward compatible for now**: `past_key_values=` / `cache_params=` are renamed to `cache` automatically, with a one-time deprecation warning. Model `forward` and `prepare_inputs_for_generation` accept the old names until **v5.40.0**, and `generate` accepts them until **v6.0.0**. Passing both an old name and `cache` raises a `ValueError`. * **Outputs too**: `outputs.past_key_values`, `outputs.cache_params` and `outputs["past_key_values"]` still return the cache. Output classes can also still be built with the old field names (e.g. `CausalLMOutputWithPast(past_key_values=...)`), so most remote-code models keep working unchanged. * **Custom code**: models defined outside the library should rename their arguments to `cache`. Layers now call `cache.update(key_states, value_states, layer_idx, kwargs=kwargs)`, so custom `Cache` subclasses that override `update` should accept the extra `kwargs` argument. 🚨 `peft>=0.22.0` is now required. 📚 Docs: ### Multimodal Outputs Generative multimodal models now return shared output classes (`MultimodalBaseModelOutputWithPast`, `MultimodalCausalLMOutputWithPast`, and their MoE variants) instead of one output class per model. Code that checks for a model-specific output class should switch to these. * 🚨 Multimodal Model Output for generative LMs (#50379) by @zucchini-nlp `modeling_attn_mask_utils.py` has been removed. Every function in it had been deprecated in favor of `transformers.masking_utils`. Remote-code models that still import `_prepare_4d_causal_attention_mask` or `AttentionMaskConverter` from it must move to `transformers.masking_utils`. ### Other things * Remove deprecated and unused older mask API file (#50728) by @Cyrilvallez LayoutLMv3 (and the PP-DocLayoutV2 reading-order model that shares its code) now go through the attention interface, so SDPA and flex attention are supported. The relative position bias is built once per forward pass and passed to attention as `position_bias`. * 🚨 LayoutLMv3: support SDPA through the attention interface, build the relative position bias once (#50688) by @14H034160212 ## Cache Beyond the rename, this release adds static-cache support to assisted decoding and fixes `generate` with flex attention and a static cache. `StaticCache` now allocates values with the value states' dtype, and the cache is kept under activation checkpointing when gradients are off. The `is_linear` / `is_croppable` properties are fixed for hybrid linear/full-attention models, BigBird block-sparse decoding works with a KV cache, and KV sharing is restored for the Gemma 4 assistants. * Support static cache in assisted decoding (#49415) by @jiqing-feng * Simplify cache handling in generate (#50910) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix generate with flex attention and a static cache (#50864) by @tarekziade * Allocate the StaticCache values with the value states' dtype (#49554) by @qgallouedec * Keep the cache under activation checkpointing when gradients are off (#50890) by @qgallouedec * [cache] Fix is_linear property to correctly remove hybrid layers (#51030) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix is_croppable property for mixed linear-full attention classes (#51028) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix BigBird block-sparse decoding with a KV cache (#49984) by @jiqing-feng * fix(gemma4): Restore KV sharing for the Gemma 4 assistants and their targets (#50531) by @harshaljanjani * Fix Dory vocabulary resizing, loop validation, and last-loop static caching (#50982) by @shan18 * Fix device placement in `test_bc_cache_name_{forward,generate}` (#50757) by @ydshieh * Update test_dynamic_cache_hard expected values for A10G (#50822) by @ydshieh ## Generation Generation fixes cover sampled beam search (candidates are sorted again before finalization), constrained sampling (batch IDs are preserved), `generate` on MPS with encoder-decoder models, and `TextStreamer`, which no longer drops spaces or lags on text without spaces such as Chinese, Japanese and Korean. `StopStringCriteria` initializes faster, and its cache now actually hits. * Restore sorting of sampled beam candidates before finalization (#50754) by @BlazeSR10hawk * fix(generate): preserve batch IDs in constrained sampling (#50883) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Fix generate for mps and encoder-decoder models (#51032) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix TextStreamer dropping spaces sometimes (#51036) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix long lagging when streaming text without spaces and NJK chars (#36708) by @CNSeniorious000 * Speed up StopStringCriteria init and fix its cache never hitting (#50780) by @TheNetherWatcher ## Continuous batching Continuous batching now works under `torch.inference_mode()` and finds sharded key/value projections under any decoder path. The per-token memory estimate scales with the TP size, warmup handles async and static inputs correctly, and an out-of-bounds error in the top-k processor is fixed. * [CB] Scale the per-token memory estimate by the TP size (#48566) by @qgallouedec * Continuous batching: find the sharded key/value projections under any decoder path (#50366) by @qgallouedec * Fix continuous batching under torch.inference_mode() (#50863) by @tarekziade * [CB] Re-order the warmup block so async warms both sets of inputs (#50868) by @remi-or * Wait for each warmup forward before the next one rewrites the static inputs (#50353) by @qgallouedec * Fix out-of-bounds error in continuous batching top-k processor (#50282) by @khush-patel-09 * [CB] Replace test prompts with less ambiguous ones (#50876) by @remi-or ## Chat templates, parsing and serving Chat parsing gets a new `python-call-list` content parser, better handling of bare keys and duplicate XML arguments, and three further parser fixes. `apply_chat_template` accepts message objects, and assistant masks are correct with left truncation. `transformers serve` handles a missing Hub cache, lists loaded models in `/v1/models`, keeps local paths containing `@`, and keeps assistant content when `tool_calls` is empty. * [Chat Parsing] Add `python-call-list` content parser (#50619) by @nico-martin * [Chat Parsing] Quote bare keys that have whitespace around them with `unquoted_keys` (#50917) by @gagan-baghel * [Chat Parsing] Preserve array values when merging duplicate XML arguments (#50760) by @crunz-ailab * Fix three chat parsing bugs (#50655) by @Rocketknight1 * Fix apply_chat_template with message objects (#50818) by @Rocketknight1 * Fix assistant tokens mask with left truncation (#50758) by @yibol9768-alt * fix(chat templating): isolate concurrent assistant tracking (#50673) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Just a small improvement in jinja (#50635) by @zucchini-nlp * Accept argument types in parentheses in get_json_schema docstrings (#50745) by @miinimal * [serve] Handle missing Hub cache and include loaded models in /v1/models (#50663) by @RyanMullins * [serve] Preserve local model paths containing '@' in ModelManager (#50662) by @RyanMullins * [serve] Keep assistant content when tool_calls is null or empty (#50707) by @AabhasK ## Pipelines Multimodal pipelines now accept media-only inputs and string assistant prefills, keep Mistral prefills in Voxtral, stop mutating generation kwargs, and return chat messages as `input_text` when returning tensors. `pipeline` also respects a `device_map` that targets a single device. * fix(pipelines): support media-only inputs in AnyToAnyPipeline (#50856) by @BlazeSR10hawk * fix(pipelines): support string assistant prefill in multimodal full-t… (#50679) by @BlazeSR10hawk * fix: preserve Mistral prefill in Voxtral and multimodal pipelines (#50624) by @BlazeSR10hawk * fix(pipelines): avoid mutating multimodal generation kwargs (#50786) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Return the chat messages as input_text when multimodal pipelines return tensors (#50816) by @burrows99 * Fix `pipeline` ignoring `device_map` when it targets a single device (#50645) by @wanhakim ## Vision Vision fixes cover Muse Glimmer's embedding order, GotOCR2 and Emu3 image sizes, Kimi video inputs, NemotronH Omni video forwarding, SAM3 RoPE precision in bf16, and DETR-family configs with `dilation=None`. SigLIP2 and LFM2-VL now process all images at once with tensor ops. Flash Attention is turned off for multimodal models whose image mask it would drop. * Fix Muse Glimmer vision embedding order (#50847) by @sid-rp * Fix GotOCR2 image size (#50810) by @guarin * Fix Emu3 image sizes after channel format conversion (#50615) by @stefanielizeth73-art * Kimi video fix (#50633) by @zucchini-nlp * Fix NemotronH_Omni_Reasoning_V3 video forwarding and MTP vision norm weight conversion (#49839) by @meatybobby * Keep SAM3's RoPE positions in fp32 when loading in bf16 (#50938) by @qgallouedec * Fix loading DETR-family configs that store dilation=None (#50934) by @sibisrinivasb * SigLIP2: compute the position-embedding resize for all images with tensor ops (#50736) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * LFM2-VL: run the projector on all images at once (#50734) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * LFM2-VL: integration expectations after #50734 (A10, MI300X) (#50923) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * Turn off Flash Attention support for multimodal models whose image mask it drops (#50724) by @albertvillanova ## Audio Audio fixes cover the OmniASR CTC blank token, Qwen3 Omni audio kwargs, Qwen3-ASR's `truncation=False` default, PeAudioVideo loading with timm 1.0.31, and the audio training examples. * Fix OmniASR CTC blank token ID (#51040) by @taking-lying-flat * Add missing past_key_values deprecation decorator to OmniASRForCondit… (#50983) by @RyanMullins * Fix Qwen3 Omni audio kwargs forwarding (#50616) by @remote-controlled-man * Restore `truncation=False` default for Qwen3-ASR audio (#50740) by @hmellor * Fixes PeAudioVideo model loading with timm 1.0.31. In that version, t… (#50862) by @sywangyi * FIx audio training examples. (#50672) by @ebezzam ## Quantization Dequantized models are now saved without the quantizer's weight conversions, and the unquantized weights of a dequantized FP8 checkpoint are cast to the model's dtype. The quantization docs also get a standard template for each method. * Save dequantized models without the quantizer's weight conversions (#50271) by @qgallouedec * Cast the unquantized weights of a dequantized FP8 checkpoint to the model's dtype (#50595) by @qgallouedec * Update inkling2 quant config (#50829) by @guarin * [docs] Standard template for quantization methods (#50848) by @stevhliu ## Parallelization FSDP2 modules are resharded before the optimizer is created, pipeline parallelism spreads layers more evenly, and TP sharding of tied weights is fixed. * Reshard FSDP2 modules before creating the optimizer (#50535) by @qgallouedec * [perf] Spread layer over PP more evenly (#50693) by @francesco-bertolotti * Fixes an issue related to TP sharding of tied weights (#50272) by @tengomucho ## Exporters Exported ONNX, OpenVINO and ExecuTorch programs load without `trust_remote_code`.
